question: What would change for me if sugary drinks were taxed?

source.title: What a sugar tax on soft drinks changes
quotes: A typical design adds 20% to the shelf price of drinks with a lot of added sugar.
Shops pass most of the tax on to customers: studies find prices rise by about 80% of the tax.
For every 10% rise in price, people buy about 12% less of the taxed drinks, according to a large review of studies.
In one country, the sugar in soft drinks sold fell by about 30% within three years, mostly because recipes changed, not because people bought fewer drinks.
Faced with the tax, many reformulate their drinks to fall below the sugar threshold.
In practice, the biggest effect often comes from companies changing recipes before the tax even starts.
It takes a larger share of income from poorer households, who drink more soft drinks.
The money raised goes to the government.

ask.question: About how many sugary soft drinks do you buy a week?
ask.help: Count regular cans and bottles, not diet ones. Zero is fine.

ask.question: What does one of those drinks usually cost?
ask.help: Check a recent receipt or the shelf price.

ask.question: How big a tax do you want to look at?
ask.help: The tax is a share added to the shelf price.

explain.caption: What changes when sugary drinks carry a tax?
The tax hits drinks with sugar above a set line.
Shops pass most of the tax on in the shelf price.
When prices rise, people buy fewer of the taxed drinks.
Drinks you still buy cost you a little more.
The tax collected goes to the government.
Drink makers can cut sugar to get under the line.
But new recipes cut more sugar than buying less does.
So the more recipes change, the less sugar people drink.
Now make it yours. Answer a few questions.

simulate.prompt: Try a bigger or smaller tax, and your own drinks.

tradeoffs: A tax cuts sugar mostly through new recipes, but drinks just under the line still contain sugar.
The money raised can fund school sport or healthy meals, but it comes most from people who drink the most.
It takes a larger share of income from poorer households, even though they may gain the most health benefit.
A bigger tax cuts more sugar, but costs regular buyers more at the till.
leftOut: How many recipes change is set by hand here; the model does not work it out from the size of the tax.
People can switch to untaxed sugary foods, which this model does not count.
The sugar cut in a changed recipe is an assumption; real cuts vary by drink and by where the line is set.
The buying response comes from a review of many studies; one country or one person can differ.
Health effects, such as weight or tooth decay, are not modelled. Tax rules and lines differ by country, so check what applies to you.
questionsToAsk: Where exactly is the sugar line, and which drinks fall under it?
Will the money raised go to anything specific, such as school sport or healthy meals?
What has happened to sugar intake in places that already have this tax?
How will the tax affect households on low incomes?
